pos: n. (the Premonstratensian abbey beside the Swale at Richmond, founded 1151, site of the Anglo-Saxon Easby Cross)
etymology: Old Norse personal name Esi with byr, a farmstead; recorded as Esebi.
biblical_def: Easby Abbey lies in the Swale valley below Richmond in North Yorkshire, founded in 1151 by Roald, constable of Richmond Castle, for Premonstratensian canons. Its remarkable survival is not the abbey but what stood on the ground before it: the Easby Cross, a carved stone cross-shaft of about the year 800, with figures of Christ and the apostles and panels of vine-scroll, now in the Victoria and Albert Museum. The abbey's own ruins preserve an unusually complete refectory, built over an undercroft with its reader's pulpit still visible in the wall. Easby was dissolved in 1536. The dictionary records Easby for the pulpit in the dining hall, which is the medieval custom of reading aloud at meals — a practice worth naming because it was right. A house that would not let men eat without hearing a text had understood something the Reformers would make general. “So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.” (Neh 8:8) describes the public reading that Nehemiah recovered, and “give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine” (1Ti 4:13) makes it an apostolic charge. The error was never the reading; it was reading in a tongue the hearers did not have.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a refectory as a room for meals in a convent; a lector as a reader; distinctly as clearly and plainly; exhortation as the act of inciting to good; and an undercroft as a vault beneath a building.
webster_full: REFECTORY, n. A room for refreshment or eating; properly, a hall or apartment in convents and other communities, where they take their meals.
READER, n. One who reads; one whose office is to read prayers or lessons in a church.
DISTINCTLY, adv. Separately; with plainness; clearly; without confusion.
EXHORTATION, n. The act or practice of exhorting; the act of inciting to laudable deeds.
VAULT, n. An arched roof, so constructed that the stones sustain each other; a cellar.
scriptures: So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
Till I come, give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine.
And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up: and, as his custom was, he went into the synagogue on the sabbath day, and stood up for to read.
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
corruption_summary: Premonstratensian abbey by the Swale at Richmond, founded 1151, with a near-complete refectory and the eighth-century Easby Cross.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is public reading. Easby's canons kept a pulpit in the dining hall; Nehemiah's Levites did the same thing on a larger scale, and the text is careful about how, “So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.” (Neh 8:8). Paul turns it into a standing charge for a minister, “give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine” (1Ti 4:13), before he says a word about eloquence.

The live temptation is to treat the practice as monastic quaintness rather than a duty. Christ himself kept it as a habit: “as his custom was, he went into the synagogue on the sabbath day, and stood up for to read” (Luk 4:16). And the apostolic aim is not performance but lodging — “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom” (Col 3:16) — which cannot happen in a language the hearer does not understand, as Easby's Latin readings could not.

pos: n. (the Augustinian priory in the West Riding, founded c. 1114, suppressed 1540)
etymology: Old English Nostel, probably the place of the hermits' nook; the early forms include Nostla.
biblical_def: Nostell Priory in the West Riding of Yorkshire began, as a number of Augustinian houses did, with hermits. A small group living in the woods near Wakefield was regularised about 1114 under the patronage of Robert de Lacy and the sponsorship of Archbishop Thurstan of York, and became a priory of canons regular dedicated to St Oswald. It was moderately endowed, held the patronage of several parish churches, and lasted without great distinction until its suppression in 1540. The site passed eventually to the Winn family, whose eighteenth-century house keeps the name. The dictionary records Nostell for that origin, because the pattern of hermits brought under a rule is the medieval church's instinct at its most revealing: solitary devotion was suspect until it was institutional. Scripture's own ordering runs the other way about. It gives the solitary man his warrant directly, “when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret” (Mat 6:6), and then gathers him not into an order but into a congregation, “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together” (Heb 10:25). A rule may be useful; it is never what makes prayer legitimate.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a canon regular as one bound by a rule; a hermit as a recluse; to regularise is not in Webster, but regular is defined as according to rule; an assembly as a company met together; and private as secluded from observation.
webster_full: REGULAR, a. Conformable to a rule, or to established forms or principles; methodical; being in accordance with a rule.
HERMITAGE, n. The habitation of a hermit; a cell or house of a recluse.
ASSEMBLY, n. A company of persons collected together in one place, and usually for some common purpose.
PRIVATE, a. Separate from others; secret; not open to the public; sequestered from company or observation.
PATRONAGE, n. Support; protection; countenance; the right of presentation to a church or ecclesiastical benefice.
scriptures: But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly.
Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
corruption_summary: Augustinian priory near Wakefield, formed about 1114 out of a company of woodland hermits, suppressed in 1540.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the order of things. Christ authorises the solitary man without reference to any institution, “when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret” (Mat 6:6), and the command is as plain and as unconditioned as “Pray without ceasing.” (1Th 5:17). No rule is required to make that prayer valid.

The live temptation is to think devotion needs regularising before it counts, which is precisely what happened to Nostell's hermits. Scripture does gather the praying man, but into the congregation and not into an order: “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together” (Heb 10:25). Within that congregation it asks for structure, “Let all things be done decently and in order.” (1Co 14:40), which is a modest thing beside a rule that reorganises a man's whole life.

“Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together” (Heb 10:25) — gathered into a congregation, not an order.
“Pray without ceasing.” (1Th 5:17) — no rule required to make it valid.

pos: n. (the Cluniac priory of St John in the West Riding, founded c. 1090, and the castle town of the cult of Thomas of Lancaster)
etymology: Latin pons fractus, the broken bridge; the local spoken form was long Pomfret.
biblical_def: Pontefract takes its name from a broken bridge and its history from a castle. The Cluniac priory of St John was founded there about 1090 by Robert de Lacy, one of the earliest Cluniac houses in the north. The town's stranger distinction is a cult: Thomas, earl of Lancaster, was executed outside Pontefract in 1322 after rebelling against Edward II, and almost at once miracles were reported at his tomb in the priory and at the hill where he died. Pilgrims came, offerings were taken, and repeated attempts were made to have him canonised — a political saint, created by his enemies' enemies. The priory was dissolved in 1539. The dictionary records Pontefract for the manufacture of that cult, which shows how quickly medieval devotion could be put to a faction's use. Scripture leaves no room for it. “God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.” (Joh 4:24) fixes worship on God and on truth together, and “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1Th 5:21) hands the test to the people rather than to the party that profits.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines canonisation as the act of declaring a man a saint; a miracle as an act exceeding human power; a relic as a remaining fragment of a saint; an offering as that presented in worship; and faction as a party in opposition.
webster_full: CANONIZE, v.t. To declare a man a saint and enroll him in the catalogue of saints.
MIRACLE, n. In theology, an event or effect contrary to the established constitution and course of things, or a deviation from the known laws of nature.
RELIC, n. That which remains; that which is left after the loss or decay of the rest; the remains of the body of a saint.
OFFERING, n. That which is presented in divine worship or religious rites; an oblation.
FACTION, n. A party, in political society, combined or acting in union, in opposition to the prince, government or state.
scriptures: God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.
Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
But when ye pray, use not vain repetitions, as the heathen do: for they think that they shall be heard for their much speaking.
Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.
corruption_summary: Cluniac priory of St John founded c. 1090, and the centre of the political cult of Thomas of Lancaster after 1322.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that worship has an object and a standard, not a sponsor. Christ states both at once: “God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.” (Joh 4:24). A cult grown up around an executed magnate satisfies neither half, whatever the offerings at the tomb amounted to.

The live temptation is to let popularity settle the question — the miracles were widely reported, therefore something was there. Paul gives the duty to the congregation instead: “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1Th 5:21). And the devotion itself drifted toward the thing Christ forbade by name, “use not vain repetitions, as the heathen do” (Mat 6:7), while the whole enterprise ran on the power Zechariah excludes, “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6).

“use not vain repetitions, as the heathen do” (Mat 6:7) — what the tomb devotion drifted into.

pos: n. (the Augustinian priory on the lower Ouse in Yorkshire, founded c. 1130)
etymology: Old Norse drag, a portage or sheltered landing place, with the plural -s; Domesday Drac.
biblical_def: Drax Priory stood by the lower Ouse in the flat country south-east of Selby, founded about 1130 by William Paynel for Augustinian canons at a place that was already a river landing. It was a middling house with a scatter of appropriated churches, and it is chiefly known to historians for a long and undignified dispute with the Paynel heirs over the advowson, and for the fact that in 1535 its income was assessed low enough to bring it under the first act of suppression; it went in 1536. Almost nothing survives above ground. The dictionary records Drax for its obscurity, which is the ordinary case. The great houses leave chronicles and the small ones leave a line in a valuation roll. Scripture is not embarrassed by that proportion. The men commended in Hebrews are a crowd of names and then not even names, “compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses” (Heb 12:1), and the promise attached to unremarkable faithfulness is unchanged: “your labour is not in vain in the Lord” (1Co 15:58). A priory that left no ruins is not thereby a wasted three hundred years, nor is it thereby justified.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an advowson as the right of presenting to a benefice; a valuation as the act of setting a price; obscure as not easily understood or little known; a witness as one who testifies; and faithful as firm in adherence to the truth.
webster_full: ADVOWSON, n. In English law, a right of presentation to a church or ecclesiastical benefice.
VALUATION, n. The act of valuing; appraisement; estimated worth or price.
OBSCURE, a. Living in darkness; hence, not noted; unknown; undistinguished; humble.
WITNESS, n. Testimony; attestation of a fact or event; that which furnishes evidence or proof.
FAITHFUL, a. Firm in adherence to the truth and to the duties of religion; true to allegiance.
scriptures: Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us,
Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
Not of works, lest any man should boast.
corruption_summary: Middling Augustinian priory by the lower Ouse, founded c. 1130 and suppressed in 1536 under the act against the lesser houses.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that most faithfulness is unrecorded. Hebrews piles up its examples and then gestures past them to a crowd it does not name, “compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses” (Heb 12:1). Paul's promise is attached to the labour and not to the record of it: “your labour is not in vain in the Lord” (1Co 15:58).

The live temptation is a sentimental one, to suppose that because a house was poor and quiet it must have been sound. Obscurity proves nothing either way. The exhortation “let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not” (Gal 6:9) is addressed to people who may well be forgotten, and the ground of their standing is the same as everyone's: “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9).

pos: n. (the small Augustinian priory of Healaugh Park near Tadcaster, regularised c. 1218)
etymology: Old English heah and leah, the high clearing; the park element is a later addition.
biblical_def: Healaugh Park Priory near Tadcaster began as a hermitage in the woods, occupied in the twelfth century by a recluse named Gilbert and then by others, and was constituted an Augustinian priory about 1218 under the patronage of the Haget family. It stayed very small. Visitation records show a community of five or six canons for much of its life, occasionally fewer, and the usual complaints of debt. It was suppressed in 1535 as one of the lesser houses, and its church furnishings were dispersed locally. The dictionary records Healaugh together with Nostell, since the two make the same point twice: the north of England was dotted with hermits, and the twelfth-century church could not leave them alone. There is nothing wrong with five men praying in a wood, and nothing holy about it either. “And he withdrew himself into the wilderness, and prayed.” (Luk 5:16) gives the practice its best precedent, and “To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world” (Jam 1:27) gives the test that a wood cannot pass on a man's behalf — a test about widows and orphans and a kept life, not about location.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a recluse as one shut up or retired from the world; a visitation as the act of a superior inspecting a church; debt as that which is owed; religion as the duty we owe to God; and unspotted as free from stain.
webster_full: RECLUSE, a. Shut up; sequestered; retired from the world or from public notice; solitary.
VISITATION, n. The act of visiting; objects of visitation; a judicial visit or official inspection of a church or religious house.
DEBT, n. That which is due from one person to another, whether money, goods or services.
RELIGION, n. The duties which we owe to God, our Creator, and the practice of all moral duties which flow from it.
UNSPOTTED, a. Free from spot; free from moral stain; unblemished; pure.
scriptures: And he withdrew himself into the wilderness, and prayed.
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
And in the morning, rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed.
Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
corruption_summary: Hermitage near Tadcaster made an Augustinian priory about 1218, never larger than a handful of canons, suppressed in 1535.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that place is not piety. Withdrawal has a good precedent, “And he withdrew himself into the wilderness, and prayed.” (Luk 5:16), and so has rising early for it, “rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed” (Mar 1:35). Both are records of what Christ did, and neither is a rule that a wood confers merit.

The live temptation is to read a hermitage as automatically the purer option. James sets the actual test, and it is not geographical: “To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world” (Jam 1:27). Nor does solitude excuse a man from the gathering, since the command stands over hermits as over everyone, “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together” (Heb 10:25).

pos: n. (the Benedictine nunnery in Swaledale, founded c. 1154, dissolved 1540)
etymology: Old Norse marr and rik or Old English ric, a boundary strip by the fen; Domesday forms include Marige.
biblical_def: Marrick Priory was founded about 1154 in Swaledale by Roger de Aske for Benedictine nuns, and it remained a small and poor community of between twelve and sixteen women for nearly four centuries. Its records are unusually ordinary: rents, a mill, a few sheep pastures, lead-mining dues in the dale, and the lists of names at each election of a prioress. It was dissolved in 1540, when the last prioress and sixteen nuns were pensioned. The church tower stands, and the buildings became a farm and later a residential centre. The dictionary records Marrick because the female houses are routinely left out of the account, and because what they offered a woman in medieval England was real: literacy, a settled community, and an alternative to marriage or service. Scripture honours the unmarried state as a calling and not as a higher order — and the Reformers' quarrel was with the vow, not the women. “Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving” (1Ti 4:3) names the error precisely, and it is an error about God's creation rather than about anyone's sincerity.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a nunnery as a house for nuns; a prioress as the female superior of a priory; a pension as an allowance for past service; celibacy as the unmarried state; and thanksgiving as the act of rendering thanks.
webster_full: NUNNERY, n. A house in which nuns reside; a cloister or retired place in which females live sequestered from the world.
PRIORESS, n. A female superior of a convent of nuns.
PENSION, n. An annual allowance of a sum of money to a person by government, or to an individual, for past services.
CELIBACY, n. An unmarried state; a single life; most frequently applied to the voluntary single life of a priest.
THANKSGIVING, n. The act of rendering thanks or expressing gratitude for favors or mercies.
scriptures: Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving of them which believe and know the truth.
Now the Spirit speaketh expressly, that in the latter times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits, and doctrines of devils;
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
Enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and into his courts with praise: be thankful unto him, and bless his name.
corruption_summary: Small Benedictine nunnery in Swaledale, founded c. 1154, dissolved 1540 with a prioress and sixteen nuns pensioned.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the quarrel was with the vow and not with the women. Paul names the thing itself, “Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving” (1Ti 4:3), and the sentence is about creation: meat and marriage are God's and are to be received. He places it in a list of predicted departures, “in the latter times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits, and doctrines of devils” (1Ti 4:1), which is a strong word and his own.

The live temptation, from either direction, is to turn Marrick's sixteen women into an argument. They were not an argument; they were a community that gave poor gentlewomen in a hard dale a literate and settled life. James' measure of religion fits them as well as anyone, “To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world” (Jam 1:27), and the gratitude Paul insists on over marriage and meat is the same gratitude the Psalter asks at the gate, “Enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and into his courts with praise” (Psa 100:4).

pos: n. (the Gloucestershire Cistercian abbey of 1246, whose relic of the Holy Blood was exposed as a counterfeit in 1539)
etymology: Old English halh in the plural, the nooks or sheltered corners; unrelated to the weather word hail.
biblical_def: Hailes Abbey in Gloucestershire was founded in 1246 by Richard, earl of Cornwall, brother of Henry III, in fulfilment of a vow made during a storm at sea. In 1270 his son Edmund gave the abbey a phial said to contain the blood of Christ, authenticated by the patriarch of Jerusalem, and Hailes became one of the chief pilgrimage destinations in England. Chaucer's Pardoner swears by it. The east end of the church was rebuilt with a ring of chapels to handle the crowds. At the dissolution in 1539 the commissioners examined the phial and reported it to be, in their account, honey coloured with saffron; the relic was destroyed and the abbey surrendered. The dictionary records Hailes as the plainest English case of a counterfeit sustained for two and a half centuries by the revenue it produced. Scripture had already shut the door on the whole trade. The blood of Christ is not a substance to be visited but a payment to be received, and “by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves” (Eph 2:8) with “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9) leaves a phial nothing to do.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a relic as the remains of a saint; a phial as a small glass vessel; counterfeit as made in imitation with a view to defraud; a vow as a solemn promise to God; and expiation as the act of atoning for a crime.
webster_full: RELIC, n. The remains of the body of a saint, or some part of his garments, preserved with a superstitious reverence.
PHIAL, n. A glass vessel or bottle; a small glass vessel used particularly for medicines.
COUNTERFEIT, a. Forged; fictitious; false; made in imitation of something else, with a view to defraud.
VOW, n. A solemn promise made to God, or by a pagan to his deity; a promise of something to be given or done.
EXPIATION, n. The act of atoning for a crime; the act of making satisfaction for an offense.
scriptures: For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Not of works, lest any man should boast.

Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ, even we have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law: for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified.
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
corruption_summary: Cistercian abbey founded 1246, home of the Holy Blood of Hailes, which the commissioners pronounced a counterfeit in 1539.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the blood of Christ is received and not visited. Hailes sold proximity to a phial, and the gospel offers the thing itself on terms that exclude purchase: “by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves” (Eph 2:8), with “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9) set immediately beside it to stop the obvious evasion.

The live temptation is to treat the fraud as an isolated abuse and the system as sound. Paul's warning is structural, not anecdotal: “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men” (Col 2:8). And the doctrine the shrine quietly denied is the one he states twice over, “a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ” (Gal 2:16), which no authentication from any patriarch could amend.

pos: n. (the Somerset abbey of Victorine canons founded c. 1170 by the earl of Gloucester)
etymology: Old English Caegin and ham, Caegin's settlement; the Avon-side form appears as Cainesham.
biblical_def: Keynsham Abbey stood between Bristol and Bath on the Avon, founded about 1170 by William, earl of Gloucester, reportedly at the dying wish of his son Robert, for canons of the Victorine congregation — Augustinians following the stricter observance of the abbey of Saint-Victor in Paris, a house famous for its school. Keynsham held churches in Somerset and in south Wales, ran a sizeable estate, and was dissolved in 1539; the buildings were almost entirely demolished and the stone carted off for local building. The dictionary records Keynsham for the Victorine connection, because Saint-Victor stood for the proposition that study and devotion belong together, and that is worth affirming without affirming the house that carried it. Hugh of Saint-Victor taught men to read; “Study to shew thyself approved unto God” (2Ti 2:15) is apostolic and so is the warning that attends it, “of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh” (Ecc 12:12). The two sentences sit side by side in the Reformed estimate of learning: necessary, and not sufficient.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a congregation as a collection or assembly; observance as the keeping of a rule; study as application of mind to books; weariness as fatigue; and doctrine as what is taught.
webster_full: CONGREGATION, n. A collection or assemblage of separate things; an assembly of persons met for the worship of God.
OBSERVANCE, n. The act of observing; performance; respect; the keeping of a custom or rule.
STUDY, n. Application of mind to books, to arts or science, or to any subject, for the purpose of learning what is not known.
WEARINESS, n. The state of being tired or fatigued; lassitude; fatigue from labor or exertion.
DOCTRINE, n. Whatever is taught; principles or positions in any science; whatever is laid down as true.
scriptures: Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
And further, by these, my son, be admonished: of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
But speak thou the things which become sound doctrine:
corruption_summary: Somerset abbey of Victorine canons founded c. 1170, dissolved 1539 and demolished almost completely for its stone.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the balance Scripture itself keeps about learning. Paul commands it, “Study to shew thyself approved unto God” (2Ti 2:15), and the Preacher qualifies it in the same breath that concedes its endlessness, “of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh” (Ecc 12:12). The Victorines were right to join the library to the choir and wrong to suppose the joining saved anyone.

The live temptation is to make scholarship the measure of a church. The measure Paul gives Titus is narrower and harder, “speak thou the things which become sound doctrine” (Tit 2:1), and the authority is located in a text rather than in a school: “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16). A house with a fine Parisian pedigree is judged by that sentence like any other.

pos: n. (the Wiltshire Augustinian nunnery founded 1232 by Ela, countess of Salisbury)
etymology: Old English lacuc, a little stream; recorded in Domesday as Lacoc.
biblical_def: Lacock Abbey in Wiltshire was founded in 1232 by Ela, countess of Salisbury, widow of William Longespee and sheriff of Wiltshire in her own right, who became its first abbess and ruled it for some twenty years. It was an Augustinian house of canonesses, comfortably endowed, and it survived to the second wave of suppressions, surrendering in 1539. The buildings were bought by Sir William Sharington, who demolished the church and converted the cloister ranges into a country house, which is why the medieval cloister, chapter house and sacristy survive almost intact under a Tudor roof. In the nineteenth century the house belonged to William Henry Fox Talbot, who made there the earliest surviving photographic negative. The dictionary records Lacock for Ela and for the oriel window Talbot photographed, and holds both without confusion. A capable widow governing a community is no scandal in Scripture; the office of abbess is simply not one Scripture knows. “To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world” (Jam 1:27) names the duty toward widows, and “Let all things be done decently and in order.” (1Co 14:40) leaves the church its government without inventing a prelacy for women or men.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an abbess as the female superior of an abbey; a canoness as a woman living under a rule; a cloister as a covered walk in a monastery; a widow as a woman who has lost her husband; and endowment as the act of settling a fund.
webster_full: ABBESS, n. A female superior or governess of a nunnery or convent of nuns.
CANONESS, n. A woman who enjoys a prebend, affixed to maids, without obligation to renounce the world.
CLOISTER, n. A monastery or nunnery; a covered passage or walk round a court, usually with a colonnade.
WIDOW, n. A woman who has lost her husband by death.
ENDOWMENT, n. The act of settling dower on a woman; the act of settling a fund or permanent provision.
scriptures: Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
Not of works, lest any man should boast.
But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:
corruption_summary: Augustinian nunnery founded 1232 by Ela, countess of Salisbury, surrendered 1539 and converted into a country house that preserved the cloister.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one James states about widows, which Ela of Salisbury both received and administered: “To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world” (Jam 1:27). That a wealthy widow should found and govern a charitable community is not the thing the Reformers objected to.

The live temptation is to make Lacock a precedent for an office. It is not one; Scripture gives the church government, “Let all things be done decently and in order.” (1Co 14:40), but names no abbess and no abbot. What it does say of every member of the house, and of the Tudor family that displaced them, is “a chosen generation, a royal priesthood” (1Pe 2:9), and of all of them alike, “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9).

pos: n. (the Wiltshire nunnery refounded 1177 as a priory of Fontevrault, retirement house of Eleanor of Provence)
etymology: Old English Ambresbyrig, the stronghold of Ambre; the name is older than the Norman refoundation.
biblical_def: Amesbury in Wiltshire had a Saxon nunnery from the tenth century, suppressed for indiscipline in 1177 and refounded in the same year as a priory of the order of Fontevrault, the French double order governed by an abbess. It became the most aristocratic nunnery in England. Eleanor of Provence, widow of Henry III, retired there and died there in 1291, and her granddaughter Mary took the veil there as a child. Amesbury was dissolved in 1539. The dictionary records Amesbury for its clientele, because the house shows what the religious life had largely become for the English nobility: a dignified retirement, a place for a surplus daughter, and a standing arrangement for prayers on the family's behalf. That last item is the one Scripture forbids outright. Prayer is not a service purchasable from professionals. “Pray without ceasing.” (1Th 5:17) is addressed to a whole church, and “when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret” (Mat 6:6) puts every believer directly before the Father with no intermediary community required or permitted.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a veil as a cover worn by nuns; a chantry as an endowment for masses; intercession as prayer on behalf of another; retirement as withdrawal from business; and a dowry as a wife's portion.
webster_full: VEIL, n. A cover; a curtain; something to intercept the view and hide an object; the habit of a nun.
CHANTRY, n. A church or chapel endowed with lands or other revenue, for the maintenance of priests to say mass for the souls of the donors.
INTERCESSION, n. Prayer or solicitation to one party in favor of another, sometimes against another.
RETIREMENT, n. The act of withdrawing from company or from public notice or station; private abode.
DOWRY, n. The money, goods or estate which a woman brings to her husband in marriage.
scriptures: But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly.
Not of works, lest any man should boast.
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
corruption_summary: Aristocratic Wiltshire nunnery of the Fontevrault order from 1177, where Eleanor of Provence retired and died in 1291.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that prayer cannot be subcontracted. Amesbury took endowments in exchange for perpetual prayers, and Paul's command is laid on everyone: “Pray without ceasing.” (1Th 5:17). Christ sends the individual to his own room and his own Father, “when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret” (Mat 6:6), which makes a paid community of intercessors unnecessary before it makes it wrong.

The live temptation is to admire the arrangement as devout philanthropy. Some of it was generous, and the nuns did real work for real neighbours, which James would count, “To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world” (Jam 1:27). But the transaction at the centre, land given for prayers that shorten a soul's punishment, collides with “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9), and no amount of charity at the gate repairs that.
